summary: Argues that IPv6 Neighbor Unreachability Detection gives up too quickly, about 3 seconds after probing starts, when a host has no alternative neighbor. It relaxes the retransmission rules so implementations can choose different timeouts depending on whether alternatives exist. It updates RFC 4861.

eli5.summary: If you knock and nobody answers, you should not give up too fast when it is your only door.

questions: why is ipv6 nud too impatient
what is the unreachable state in ipv6 neighbor discovery
subtitle: IPv6 hosts give up on a silent neighbor too fast; this RFC lets them keep trying, with backoff.

tldr.problem: IPv6 Neighbor Unreachability Detection discards a neighbor after three probes one second apart. That is too impatient when the host has no alternative neighbor, and a brief outage then triggers extra multicast traffic.
tldr.mechanism: A new UNREACHABLE state keeps the cached link-layer address and keeps probing with multicast Neighbor Solicitations on an exponentially backing-off timer, instead of discarding the entry.
tldr.outcome: Neighbor Discovery becomes as robust as IPv4 ARP when there is only one neighbor to talk to, while hosts with alternatives can still switch quickly. It updates RFC 4861.

today: RFC 7048 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4861. No later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why NUD Is Too Impatient
sections.content:
Neighbor Unreachability Detection (NUD) is the part of IPv6 Neighbor Discovery that notices when a neighbor stops being reachable. By default it sends three transmissions spaced one second apart before giving up.

Those short timeouts make sense when a host has an alternative: another router in its Default Router List, or a Neighbor Cache Entry (NCE) created by a Redirect message. The host just redoes next-hop selection and moves on. When there is no alternative, the same short timeout is a weakness.

Giving up on the entry makes the next packet trigger multicast Neighbor Solicitations every second instead of unicast ones. Transient problems such as spanning tree reconvergence, which can take many seconds to resolve, then cause extra multicast load on the network.
sections.eli5: Giving up fast is fine if you have another friend to ask. If this friend is the only one, giving up fast just makes everyone shout across the room.

sections.title: Comparison with ARP and Test Suites
sections.content:
The RFC says IPv6 Neighbor Discovery is operationally more brittle than the IPv4 Address Resolution Protocol (ARP). For IPv4 there is no mandatory time limit on ARP retransmission, so implementors can pick more robust schemes.

The RFC also notes that the constants MAX_MULTICAST_SOLICIT, MAX_UNICAST_SOLICIT and RETRANS_TIMER from RFC 4861 appear to have been made part of IPv6 conformance testing. That strictness is consistent with RFC 4861, so the standard itself has to change to allow more robust behavior. Further motivation is covered in RFC 6583.
sections.eli5: The older address-asking system let people be patient, but the newer one had a strict stopwatch. This RFC loosens the stopwatch.

sections.title: The UNREACHABLE State
sections.content:
The core change is a new UNREACHABLE state in the conceptual model of RFC 4861. An NCE in this state keeps its link-layer address, and IPv6 packets continue to be sent to that address. The NUD Neighbor Solicitations in this state are multicast to the solicited-node multicast address, on a timeout that follows an exponential backoff.

Wherever RFC 4861 says to discard the NCE after N probes (Sections 7.3 and 7.3.3, and Appendix C), the entry now moves to UNREACHABLE instead. Apart from multicast instead of unicast and the backoff, UNREACHABLE works like the PROBE state.

If the entry came from a Redirect, a node MAY delete it instead, and SHOULD NOT use a Redirect-created entry for sending while it is UNREACHABLE. In router selection, an UNREACHABLE router is not known to be reachable, so the text "in any state other than INCOMPLETE" becomes "in any state other than INCOMPLETE or UNREACHABLE".
sections.eli5: Instead of crossing the neighbor off your list, you put a sticky note on them that says "not answering right now". You still remember where they live and keep checking, a little less often each time.

sections.title: State Table Changes
sections.content:
The RFC replaces one row of the RFC 4861 Appendix C table. A PROBE entry that hits the retransmit timeout after N retransmissions used to be discarded. Now it increases the timeout, sends a multicast NS and moves to UNREACHABLE. An UNREACHABLE entry that hits the retransmit timeout increases the timeout, sends a multicast NS and stays UNREACHABLE.

One non-obvious edit: in the case "NA, Solicited=1, Override=0, different link-layer address than cached", UNREACHABLE is added to the list of STALE, PROBE or DELAY, so the entry is unchanged. Other transitions already say "not INCOMPLETE" and need no change.
sections.eli5: The rule book gets one new line: when the waiting runs out, move to the "not answering" note and keep trying, rather than tearing up the page.

sections.title: Backoff, Multicast and Garbage Collection
sections.content:
If an implementation sends more than MAX_UNICAST_SOLICIT or MAX_MULTICAST_SOLICIT packets, it SHOULD use exponential backoff of the retransmit timer, so that a steady background of retransmissions does not add significant load. The backoff SHOULD be clamped at a reasonable maximum such as 60 seconds (MAX_RETRANS_TIMER).

If no IPv6 packet is sent using an UNREACHABLE NCE, it is RECOMMENDED to stop retransmitting the multicast NS until the entry is garbage collected or traffic uses it again. A node can unicast the first few solicitations while UNREACHABLE, but it MUST switch to multicast within 60 seconds of the initial retransmission, so it can detect a changed link-layer address for the target.

Nodes may still garbage collect any NCE at any time, and MAY prefer to collect UNREACHABLE ones first.
sections.eli5: You wait longer between knocks each time, but never longer than a minute. And if nobody needs that door, you stop knocking altogether.

sections.title: The Example Algorithm
sections.content:
Section 4 is not normative. It gives a simple algorithm driven by operator-configurable values: MAX_UNICAST_SOLICIT, MAX_MULTICAST_SOLICIT, RETRANS_TIMER, plus the new BACKOFF_MULTIPLE, MAX_RETRANS_TIMER and MARK_UNREACHABLE. The next delay is the backoff multiple raised to the retransmission number, times the retransmit timer, times a random jitter factor so hosts do not synchronize.

With MAX_UNICAST_SOLICIT=5, RETRANS_TIMER=1, MAX_RETRANS_TIMER=60, BACKOFF_MULTIPLE=3 and MARK_UNREACHABLE=3, retransmissions occur at 1, 4, 13 and 40 seconds after the first transmission. The entry is marked UNREACHABLE at 4 seconds (compared to 2 seconds with the fixed scheme in RFC 4861), and after 5 transmissions, 40 seconds in, the node switches to multicast probes.

Setting BACKOFF_MULTIPLE=1, MARK_UNREACHABLE=3 and MAX_UNICAST_SOLICIT=3 reproduces the RFC 4861 behavior. The RFC states the 60 second maximum is consistent with DHCPv6.
sections.eli5: Knock right away, then after 1 second, then 3 more, then 9, then 27. The waits grow quickly so you do not pester, and a little randomness stops everyone from knocking at once.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says relaxing the retransmission behavior for NUD is believed to have no impact on security. In particular it does not affect the application of Secure Neighbor Discovery (RFC 3971).
sections.eli5: Waiting a bit longer before giving up does not open any new way for bad guys to get in.
